content: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is characterized by the persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the bloodstream for a minimum duration of six months. However, interpreting HBV serological markers is a complex process. The most commonly utilized serological tests for HBV diagnosis include HBsAg, total anti-HBc (antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen), and anti-HBs (antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen). Testing strategies often involve sequential testing, such as HBsAg detection followed by hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) or nucleic acid testing (NAT). HBsAg detection can be performed using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or immunoassays. RDTs designed for screening purposes include various formats such as solid-phase assays, flow-through assays, agglutination tests, and lateral-flow assays. Among these, immunochromatographic assays are the most prevalent. Immunoassays for HBsAg detection employ either polyclonal or monoclonal anti-HBs antibodies. These assays utilize labeling techniques to measure antigen-antibody complexes, which may involve radioactive compounds, enzymes that induce color changes in solution, or substances that emit light. Advancements in HBV detection technologies have created new opportunities to improve screening, referral, and treatment processes. Existing systematic reviews on hepatitis B testing have primarily focused on point-of-care (POC) tests, including those with unclear reference standards or those unsuitable for assessing operational diagnostic accuracy in real-world settings. The objective of this review was to identify quantitative evidence regarding the sensitivity and specificity of assays used to detect hepatitis B antibodies, synthesize this evidence, and inform diagnostic models. To our knowledge, this is the first study to comprehensively compare the clinical performance of both RDTs and laboratory-based immunoassays, specifically addressing diagnostic accuracy in the context of HIV co-infection. The primary research question (PICO framework) was: Among individuals identified for hepatitis B testing, what is the diagnostic accuracy of available assays for detecting HBsAg? The population (P) included individuals undergoing HBV testing. The intervention (I) involved the use of RDTs or immunoassays for HBsAg detection. The comparator (C) was a reference standard comprising laboratory-based enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), with or without neutralization for confirmation. The outcome (O) was diagnostic accuracy, measured in terms of sensitivity, specificity, true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). A sub-analysis was conducted to compare the accuracy of HBsAg assays against a nucleic acid amplification test (NAT) reference standard. The literature search strategy was developed by a medical librarian with expertise in systematic review methodologies. Databases searched included MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Science Citation Index Expanded, SCOPUS, and others. The search was supplemented by contacting researchers, experts, and authors of major trials to identify unpublished or in-press manuscripts. The review was registered in PROSPERO and adhered to PRISMA guidelines. Study selection involved three stages: initial screening of titles/abstracts by a single reviewer, independent full-text review by two reviewers, and resolution of discrepancies through discussion or a third independent reviewer. Inclusion criteria encompassed case-control, cross-sectional, cohort studies, and randomized trials evaluating HBsAg tests published up to May 2015. Exclusion criteria included conference abstracts, commentaries, reviews, studies not focused on sensitivity and specificity, and non-English articles. Eligible studies included original data from patient specimens across all age groups, settings, and countries. Specimen types included whole blood (venous and capillary), plasma, and serum. Studies using commercial HBsAg tests were included, while in-house tests and outdated laboratory-based immunoassays were excluded. Reference standards for definitive HBV diagnosis included commercially available immunoassays or NATs. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers and included variables such as study design, sample size, specimen type, reference standard, and raw diagnostic data (TP, TN, FP, FN). The QUADAS-2 tool was used to assess bias, and the GRADE system was applied to evaluate the strength of evidence. Meta-analysis was conducted using standard methods for diagnostic accuracy, calculating pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (PLR), and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) with 95% confidence intervals. The DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model was employed due to significant heterogeneity among studies. Subgroup analyses were performed based on study year, geographical area, test type, specimen type, and patient characteristics. A total of 11,589 citations were identified, with 6,575 duplicates removed. After screening, 33 studies were included in the final analysis. These studies originated from 23 countries and evaluated both RDTs and laboratory-based immunoassays against reference standards. Sample sizes ranged from 25 to 3,928 individuals. The majority of studies were conducted in laboratory settings, with some performed in field conditions. Specimen types included serum, plasma, capillary, and whole blood. The findings highlight the diagnostic accuracy of HBsAg assays, with implications for improving HBV screening and management strategies globally.
